lessons.title: How the Stock Market Actually Works

blocks.robotComment: Investing Fundamentals covered what a stock is. This track is about the marketplace where they actually change hands. 🏛️
blocks.body: A stock exchange is a marketplace where buyers and sellers meet to trade shares of publicly listed companies — the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) and Nasdaq are the two biggest examples in the United States, and most countries have their own. Nobody physically hands over paper certificates anymore; it's all electronic, matching millions of buy and sell orders every single day.

Every company traded on an exchange has a ticker symbol: a short, unique code used to look it up and trade it, like AAPL for Apple or MSFT for Microsoft. Instead of typing out a full company name every time, traders and investors just use the ticker.

code.code:
AAPL  →  Apple Inc.
MSFT  →  Microsoft Corporation
KO    →  The Coca-Cola Company
code.caption: A ticker is just a short, unique nickname for trading a specific company's stock.

blocks.sentence: A short, unique code used to look up and trade a specific company's stock, like AAPL for Apple, is called a ___.
blocks.explanation: The ticker symbol is the shorthand code an exchange assigns to a company so it can be quickly identified and traded.

blocks.robotComment: This matching happens in a fraction of a second, millions of times a day. ⚡
blocks.body: At the core of every exchange is order matching: someone willing to buy states the price they'll pay, someone willing to sell states the price they want, and when those two prices meet, a trade happens instantly. Modern exchanges run this matching electronically, at massive speed and scale, which is why a trade you place today usually executes within moments.

blocks.question: What is a stock exchange?
options: A marketplace where buyers and sellers trade shares of publicly listed companies
A single company that sells its own stock directly to one buyer
blocks.explanation: An exchange is the marketplace itself — it doesn't own the companies traded on it, it just matches buyers and sellers.

blocks.statement: Every publicly traded company has its own unique ticker symbol.
blocks.explanation: Ticker symbols are unique on a given exchange, which is exactly what makes them a reliable shorthand for looking up and trading a specific company.

lessons.title: Who's on the Other Side of Your Trade?

blocks.robotComment: Every trade needs someone on the other side of it. Ever wonder who that actually is? 🤔
blocks.body: Whenever you buy a share, someone else is selling it to you — and whenever you sell, someone else is buying. That other side is usually one of two things: another everyday investor placing an order through their own brokerage, or a market maker, a firm whose whole job is standing ready to buy or sell almost any listed stock at any moment.

Market makers exist to provide liquidity: the ability to buy or sell quickly without waiting around for a matching order to show up on its own. In exchange for constantly offering to trade, they profit from the small difference between the price they'll buy at and the price they'll sell at — a gap called the bid-ask spread.

blocks.sentence: The ability to buy or sell a stock quickly, without waiting for a matching order, is called ___.
blocks.explanation: Liquidity is exactly this: how easily and quickly something can be bought or sold near its current price.

blocks.robotComment: A widely-traded stock like Apple has enormous liquidity — a small, obscure company might not. 📉
blocks.body: Not every stock is equally liquid. A large, well-known company traded by millions of people has extremely high liquidity — orders get matched almost instantly. A small, thinly-traded company might have far fewer buyers and sellers at any given moment, meaning trades can take longer and prices can jump more with each one.

blocks.question: What does a market maker's role actually involve?
options: Standing ready to buy or sell a stock almost constantly, providing liquidity to the market
Setting the exact price every stock must trade at
Approving which companies are allowed to list on an exchange
blocks.explanation: Market makers keep markets liquid by continuously offering to buy and sell, profiting from the small bid-ask spread in return.

blocks.statement: Every stock on an exchange has exactly the same level of liquidity.
blocks.explanation: Liquidity varies a lot — large, widely-held companies trade far more easily than small, thinly-traded ones.

blocks.robotComment: Same marketplace, two very different games. Worth being honest about which one you're actually playing. 🎯
blocks.body: Investing means buying shares of companies you believe in and holding them for years or decades, letting the business grow and compound in value over time — the approach covered in the Investing Fundamentals track. Trading means buying and selling more actively, often within days, hours, or even minutes, trying to profit from short-term price movements instead of a company's long-term growth.

Both use the exact same marketplace and the exact same mechanics — orders, tickers, exchanges — which is what this track teaches. But they demand very different things from the person doing them. Investing mostly rewards patience and consistency. Trading demands constant attention, quick decisions, and a much higher tolerance for being wrong, since prices can move against you in seconds.

blocks.sentence: Buying and selling shares actively, often within days or hours, to profit from short-term price moves, is called ___.
blocks.explanation: Trading is the shorter-term activity — investing is the longer-term, "buy and hold" approach.

blocks.robotComment: This isn't a warning to scare you off — it's just honest framing before we go further. 🧭
blocks.body: It's worth being upfront about this early: research consistently shows most active traders underperform a simple long-term investing approach, once trading costs and mistakes are factored in. That doesn't mean learning how trading actually works is a waste — understanding order types, charts, and market mechanics makes you a sharper investor too, even if you never place a single short-term trade.

blocks.question: What is the main difference between investing and trading?
options: Investing holds for the long term expecting company growth; trading buys and sells more actively for short-term price moves
They are two names for the exact same thing
Investing only applies to bonds, trading only applies to stocks
Trading always guarantees a profit, investing does not
blocks.explanation: Both use the same markets and mechanics, but the time horizon and what each is trying to profit from are fundamentally different.

blocks.statement: Most active traders end up beating a simple long-term investing approach once costs and mistakes are accounted for.
blocks.explanation: The evidence points the other way: most active traders underperform simple long-term investing once real-world costs and mistakes are included.

blocks.robotComment: That number can change dozens of times before you even finish reading it. ⚡
blocks.body: The big number next to any stock ticker is the current price — the price at which the most recent trade actually happened. It isn't a fixed, guaranteed price; it's a snapshot that updates constantly while the market is open, changing every time a new trade executes.

Alongside the current price, most quotes also show the day range: the lowest and highest prices the stock has traded at so far during today's session. A wide day range usually means a more volatile day; a narrow one means the price has stayed fairly calm.

code.caption: The day range shows the floor and ceiling the price has touched so far today — not where it will end up.

blocks.sentence: The lowest and highest prices a stock has traded at so far during today's session is called the ___.
blocks.explanation: The day range captures the full spread between today's low and today's high, showing how much the price has moved.

blocks.robotComment: This is exactly why the bid and ask prices, covered next, matter so much. 🔍
blocks.body: It's easy to assume the current price is exactly what you'll pay if you buy right now, but by the time your order reaches the market, the price may have already ticked up or down slightly. That's completely normal — it's just how a constantly-updating marketplace works.

blocks.question: What does a stock's 'current price' actually represent?
options: The price at which the most recent trade happened
A guaranteed price for your next trade
The average price over the past year
A price set once per day by the exchange
blocks.explanation: The current price is simply the price of the last executed trade — it updates continuously as new trades happen.

blocks.statement: The current price shown on a quote guarantees the exact price you'll pay if you buy right now.
blocks.explanation: The current price reflects the last trade, not a locked-in price — by the time your order executes, the price may have moved slightly.

blocks.robotComment: Same idea from Level 1's bid-ask spread — now shown right on the quote screen. 🔎
blocks.body: Level 1 introduced the bid-ask spread through market makers. On an actual quote screen, you'll see this directly as two separate prices sitting side by side: the bid price and the ask price.

The bid is the highest price any buyer is currently willing to pay for the stock. The ask (sometimes called the offer) is the lowest price any seller is currently willing to accept. If you want to buy immediately, you generally pay the ask; if you want to sell immediately, you generally receive the bid.

code.caption: Buyers offer the bid, sellers ask for the ask — the small gap between them is the spread.

blocks.sentence: The highest price a buyer is currently willing to pay for a stock is called the ___.
blocks.explanation: The bid is the buyer's offer — the price sellers can accept to sell immediately.

blocks.robotComment: A one-cent spread on a huge company versus a dollar-wide spread on an obscure one — same idea as Level 1's liquidity lesson. 💧
blocks.body: The gap between the bid and the ask is the spread, and it tends to shrink for heavily-traded, liquid stocks and widen for thinly-traded ones. A tighter spread generally means it's cheaper to get in and out of a position quickly.

blocks.question: If you place an order to buy a stock immediately, which price do you generally pay?
options: The average of the day's high and low
blocks.explanation: Buying immediately generally means paying the ask — the lowest price any seller is currently willing to accept.

blocks.statement: The ask price is generally the price you receive when selling a stock immediately.
blocks.explanation: Selling immediately generally gets you the bid price, not the ask — the ask is what buyers pay.

blocks.robotComment: Price tells you what happened. Volume tells you how much everyone actually cared. 📊
blocks.body: Trading volume is simply the number of shares that changed hands over a given period, usually shown for the current trading day. It's a headcount of activity, separate from price entirely — a stock can have a huge volume while barely moving in price, or a tiny volume while swinging wildly.

Volume is usually compared to a stock's average volume — its typical daily amount — rather than judged as a raw number on its own. A large, popular company might normally trade tens of millions of shares a day, while a small company might normally trade only a few thousand.

code.caption: Volume more than double the average usually signals unusually high interest in the stock that day.

blocks.sentence: The number of shares that changed hands over a given period, like a trading day, is called ___.
blocks.explanation: Volume is simply a headcount of shares traded — it says nothing about direction, only about activity.

blocks.body: Unusually high volume often shows up around news, earnings reports, or other events that make a lot of people want to trade at once — it's a sign that something changed. Unusually low volume can mean fewer people are paying attention, which can also mean it's harder to buy or sell quickly without moving the price.

blocks.question: What does trading volume actually measure?
options: The number of shares that changed hands over a given period
The exact direction the price is moving
The company's total profit for the year
The number of investors who own the stock forever
blocks.explanation: Volume is a pure headcount of shares traded — it doesn't by itself say whether the price went up or down.

blocks.statement: A spike in trading volume well above average often lines up with news or other events affecting the stock.
blocks.explanation: Unusual volume is frequently a sign that new information — earnings, news, or other events — has pushed more people to trade at once.

questions.question: What does a stock's current price represent?

blocks.robotComment: Two companies can have the same share price and wildly different market caps — the share count is the missing piece. 🧩
blocks.body: Market capitalization, or market cap, is the total market value of a company's entire outstanding stock. It's calculated with one simple formula: share price multiplied by the total number of shares outstanding.

A company with a $50 share price and 2 billion shares outstanding has a far larger market cap than a company with a $200 share price but only 10 million shares outstanding. Share price alone tells you almost nothing about a company's actual size.

code.code:
Market Cap = Share Price x Shares Outstanding

Share price:          $50
Shares outstanding:    2,000,000,000
----------------------------------
Market Cap = $50 x 2,000,000,000 = $100,000,000,000
code.caption: A $50 stock with 2 billion shares outstanding has a $100 billion market cap.

blocks.sentence: Market capitalization is calculated as share price multiplied by total shares ___.
blocks.explanation: Market cap equals share price times the number of shares outstanding — the total shares actually issued and held by investors.

blocks.robotComment: Same size label doesn't mean same risk level, but it's a useful starting sort. 🗂️
blocks.body: Market cap is why companies get grouped into rough size categories, like large-cap, mid-cap, and small-cap — labels that describe overall size and, generally, how much the stock's price tends to swing. Larger companies tend to be more stable and closely watched; smaller companies can be more volatile but also less thoroughly studied by the market.

blocks.question: A company has a $40 share price and 5 billion shares outstanding. What is its market capitalization?

blocks.statement: A higher share price always means a company has a larger market capitalization than one with a lower share price.
blocks.explanation: Market cap depends on share price multiplied by shares outstanding — a lower-priced stock with far more shares outstanding can easily have a larger market cap.

blocks.robotComment: Think of the day range as today's weather and the 52-week range as the whole year's climate. 🌦️
blocks.body: The 52-week high and 52-week low are the highest and lowest prices a stock has traded at over the past full year. Unlike the day range, which resets every morning, this range gives you a much longer view of how much a stock's price has actually moved recently.

Where the current price sits within that 52-week range can add useful context. A price sitting near its 52-week high suggests recent strength; a price sitting near its 52-week low suggests recent weakness — though neither one, by itself, tells you what happens next.

code.caption: This price sits close to its 52-week high, meaning it's trading near the top of its past year's range.

blocks.sentence: The highest and lowest prices a stock has traded at over the past full year make up its ___ range.
blocks.explanation: The 52-week range covers a full year of trading, giving much more context than the single-day range.

blocks.robotComment: A price level alone never explains why it got there. 🧠
blocks.body: It's tempting to treat a new 52-week high as a warning sign that a stock is now too expensive, or a 52-week low as an automatic bargain. Neither assumption holds up on its own — a stock at a 52-week high can keep climbing for solid reasons, and a stock at a 52-week low can keep falling for equally solid ones.

highlights.text: Neither assumption holds up on its own

blocks.question: What does the 52-week high and low actually show?
options: The highest and lowest prices the stock has traded at over the past year
The exact price the stock will reach next
The number of shares traded today only
blocks.explanation: The 52-week range is purely historical — the highest and lowest traded prices over the trailing 12 months.

blocks.statement: A stock trading at a new 52-week high is guaranteed to fall back down soon.
blocks.explanation: A 52-week high is just a historical marker — it says nothing on its own about what the price will do next.

blocks.robotComment: It's a starting point for a conversation, not a final verdict on a stock. ⚖️
blocks.body: The price-to-earnings ratio, or P/E ratio, compares a company's share price to how much profit it earns per share. It's one of the most commonly quoted numbers for getting a rough sense of how expensive a stock looks relative to its actual earnings.

The formula divides the current share price by earnings per share, or EPS: the company's profit divided across every share outstanding. A P/E of 20 means investors are currently paying $20 for every $1 of the company's annual earnings.

code.code:
P/E Ratio = Share Price / Earnings Per Share

Share price:          $60
Earnings per share:    $3
----------------------------
P/E = $60 / $3 = 20
code.caption: A P/E of 20 means the market is pricing this stock at 20 times its annual earnings per share.

blocks.sentence: The P/E ratio divides a company's share price by its earnings ___ share.
blocks.explanation: P/E stands for price-to-earnings — share price divided by earnings per share.

blocks.robotComment: A number this popular still can't do all the thinking for you. 🤨
blocks.body: A high P/E can mean investors expect strong future growth, or it can mean the stock is simply overpriced relative to what the company actually earns right now — the number alone can't tell you which. A low P/E can mean a genuine bargain, or it can mean the market has real doubts about the company's future earnings. P/E is a useful starting question, never a final answer, and it's most meaningful when compared against similar companies in the same industry.

highlights.text: a useful starting question, never a final answer

blocks.question: A stock trades at $90 per share with earnings per share of $6. What is its P/E ratio?
blocks.explanation: $90 divided by $6 earnings per share equals a P/E ratio of 15.

blocks.statement: A high P/E ratio always means a stock is a bad investment.
blocks.explanation: A high P/E can reflect real growth expectations, not necessarily overpricing — it's only one data point, not a verdict on its own.
